transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I... I guess I'm here because things have been getting a bit strange at work. I'm a surveillance officer at the casino, you know, watching the monitors all night. It's usually pretty quiet, especially on the graveyard shift. I used to love the quiet, actually. Reminds me of when I was a kid and we'd go up to the cabin in the summer... just the sound of the crickets and nothing else. My brother used to try and catch them in jars, but I always felt bad for them. Anyway, what scared me enough to actually come in here is that lately, during those quiet stretches in the surveillance room, I've been hearing voices. They come right through the monitor speakers, even when I have every single channel completely muted. They say things to me, like, "You missed it, Ruth," or "People are going to get hurt because of you." It's terrifying. And the worst part is, the other guards don't hear a thing when they walk by. It's just me. I don't know what's happening.
What kind of things do the voices typically say to you, are they mostly critical or do they tell you to do something?

Well, like I mentioned, they mostly just say those terrible things... that I missed something, or that it's my fault people are going to get hurt. They don't really order me around, they just... they blame me. And it's always coming through those monitor speakers when the channels are completely muted. 

I actually had Gary from IT come look at the wiring last week. Gary's always eating those little powdered donuts, you know? He leaves white dust all over the control panels. I keep telling him he's going to ruin the switchboards, but he just brushes it off. He's been working at the casino for, gosh, maybe fifteen years? Since before they put in the new slot machines by the buffet. The old ones used to pay out in actual coins, and the sound was just deafening when you walked the floor... just metal clinking all night long. I kind of miss the coins, honestly. The paper vouchers just don't feel the same when people win. 

But anyway, Gary checked the speakers and said the audio feeds were completely dead when I mute them. There's no signal at all. So... yeah, they don't tell me what to do, they just criticize me. And I'm the only one who hears it.
Do you hear the voices only when you're at work in the surveillance room, or do you hear them at other times and places as well?

It's just at work. Just in that room. Like I was saying, it's during those quiet stretches in the surveillance room when I hear them coming right through the monitor speakers. "You missed it, Ruth," or "People are going to get hurt because of you." Even when every channel is completely muted and no one else hears a thing. I try to stay busy when it gets quiet, you know, looking at the different camera angles. We have this one camera that points right at the craps table in the high-roller area. I like watching the dealers there. They have these really specific hand movements when they clear the dice, it's almost like a dance. My cousin took tap dancing lessons for years when we were kids. She had these shiny black shoes with the metal plates on the bottom, and she'd practice on the linoleum floor in her kitchen. Her mom hated it, said it sounded like a hail storm inside the house. I always wanted to try it, but I was too clumsy. Anyway, yeah, it's only in the surveillance room when I'm at the monitors.
Do the voices you hear sound like they are coming from people you know or are they completely unfamiliar?

I don't know, they don't really sound like anyone I know. They're just... voices. Unfamiliar, I guess. It's hard to place them because they sound a little metallic, coming through the speakers like that. It reminds me of the drive-thru speaker at this old fast food place I used to go to after my late shifts when I first started working security. The microphone was always broken, so the person taking your order sounded like they were talking underwater. I used to get their double cheeseburger and a vanilla milkshake. You know, they changed the recipe for the milkshakes a few years ago. Now they just taste artificial, like they just dump a bunch of syrup in there instead of using real ice cream. It's a shame. Food just isn't made the same way anymore, everything is so processed. My grandmother used to make everything from scratch. Her Sunday roasts were incredible. But anyway, no, the voices don't sound like anyone from my life.
Are the voices constant when you're in the surveillance room, or do they come and go?

They come and go. It's really just during those quiet stretches in the surveillance room. That's actually what scared me enough to finally come in and see you... hearing those voices coming through the monitor speakers when it gets dead quiet in there. "You missed it, Ruth," or "People are going to get hurt because of you." Even when every channel is completely muted and no one else hears a thing. 

It gets so quiet in there sometimes you can hear the hum of the fluorescent lights. We have those long tube lights, and one of them has been flickering for weeks. It drives me absolutely crazy. I keep putting in maintenance requests, but you know how it is. They prioritize the casino floor because that's where the money is. If a light goes out over a blackjack table, they fix it in five minutes. But back in the offices? You could be sitting in the dark for a month. My uncle used to be an electrician, actually. He wired his whole house himself. He even built this elaborate model train set in his basement with all these tiny streetlights and railroad crossings that actually lit up and dinged. He spent thousands of hours down there... he hand-painted all the little people waiting at the stations. I used to love watching the trains go around when I was little. But yeah, the voices aren't constant. Just when it gets quiet.
Do you see anything unusual when you're in the surveillance room, like shadows or movements that aren't really there?

No, I haven't really noticed anything like that. No shadows or... things that aren't there on the screens. It's just the voices. I mean, I stare at those screens for hours, so sometimes your eyes play tricks on you, just from the strain, you know? Like you'll see a little blur, but it's just a smudge on the glass or someone walking by really fast. They make us use these special cleaning wipes for the monitors, but they always leave streaks. It's like trying to clean a window with a greasy rag. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she swears by using newspaper and vinegar to clean her windows. She says it's the only thing that doesn't leave streaks. She's got this big bay window in her front room, and she sits there all day with her cat, just watching the street. The cat's name is Barnaby, he's this huge orange tabby. He must weigh twenty pounds. He just sleeps on the back of the sofa, right in the sun. I tried to pet him once and he swatted at me. Some cats are just mean like that, I guess. But no, I don't see anything unusual on the cameras. Just the regular casino stuff.
Have the voices you're hearing affected your ability to do your job or interact with others at work?

Well, yeah, they have. I mean, I'm just so distracted and... worn down. I've already made mistakes on my shift paperwork, which is so unlike me. I used to be so meticulous about the logs. My supervisor even pointed it out last week. And I've had to step back from, you know, my friends and the people I usually talk to on shift, because I just can't keep up the way I used to. It's like I don't have the energy for conversations anymore. 

Even at home, I'm just getting through the bare minimum. I don't cook anymore, I don't invite anyone over, I haven't touched any of my projects around the house. Speaking of projects, I started re-caulking my bathtub about a month ago. I bought this special mold-resistant silicone caulk from the hardware store. The guy working there, he had this huge bushy beard, like a lumberjack or something. He told me I needed a specific kind of caulking gun so my hands wouldn't cramp up. I bought it, but it's still sitting in the plastic bag under the sink. I just look at it sometimes and think about doing it, but... I don't know. My dad used to fix everything around the house. He built us this incredible treehouse when I was a kid, with a rope ladder and a trapdoor. We used to spend all summer up there, reading comic books and eating popsicles. The cherry ones always stained your fingers red for days. But yeah... I just do the basics now. Work, sleep, that's about it.
How do you feel when you hear the voices criticizing you?

I just feel... awful. Like they're right. I keep replaying every missed camera angle or delayed call in my head, like it's proof that I'm just careless. Dangerous, even. And part of me really believes I deserve to be punished if anything goes wrong on my watch. It's this heavy, sinking feeling in my chest. 

It reminds me of this one time when I was in college, I lost my roommate's dog. She asked me to watch him for just an hour while she went to a study group. He was this little terrier mix, scruffy, always full of energy. His name was Buster. Anyway, I left the front door cracked open while I was grabbing the mail, and he just bolted. I spent three hours running around the neighborhood crying, shaking a bag of treats. We finally found him at the park two blocks over, chasing ducks into the pond. He was completely soaked and smelled terrible, like algae and mud. My roommate was so mad at me, she wouldn't speak to me for a week. She ended up moving out at the end of the semester. She transferred to a school out of state, actually. Somewhere in Colorado, I think. She always wanted to learn how to snowboard. But yeah, when I hear those voices at work, it's that same feeling. Like I'm just waiting for the disaster that's entirely my fault.
Do you ever think that the voices or the criticism you're hearing might be related to some kind of plot or conspiracy against you?

No, I don't think it's a plot or... a conspiracy or anything like that. It's just me. I mean, they're just pointing out what's already true, that I'm messing up. Why would anyone need a conspiracy for that? It's all on me. 

Speaking of conspiracies, though, my brother used to be obsessed with them. He had this whole corkboard in his bedroom when we were teenagers, covered in printouts and red string. He was convinced the moon landing was faked on a soundstage in Nevada. He even bought this telescope, a really nice one, saved up his allowance for months. He said he was going to look for the rover tracks himself. He used to drag me out into the backyard at two in the morning in the freezing cold, making me look through the lens. You couldn't see anything but craters, obviously. He's an accountant now, if you can believe it. Lives in Ohio with his wife and three kids. They just got a golden retriever puppy. Those dogs are so cute when they're little, but they chew on everything. My cousin had one that ate an entire leather shoe once. Had to take it to the emergency vet and everything. Cost her like two thousand dollars. But no, I don't think anyone is plotting against me at the casino. It's just my own failures catching up with me.
Have you ever experienced any other times in your life when you heard voices or saw things that weren't there?

No, never. I mean, before all this started... before this whole stretch of feeling just so hopeless and guilty after they changed the surveillance lead at work, I never experienced anything like this. I've never heard accusations coming through the headsets or the monitors, and I definitely never felt so certain that I was this dangerous person who was going to get people hurt. The voices and... and believing all these awful things about myself, it all just seems to be part of this same low period I'm stuck in right now. 

It's funny, though, talking about hearing things... when I was in my twenties, I lived in this really old apartment building downtown. The walls were paper thin. I swear, I could hear my neighbor's entire life. He was this older guy, Mr. Henderson. He used to listen to these old radio shows, like the mystery ones from the 1940s, on full blast every Sunday night. The Shadow, I think it was called? "Who knows what evil lurks in the hearts of men?" That whole thing. It used to drive me crazy when I was trying to study for my finals. I was taking this abnormal psychology class as an elective—which was so hard, by the way, the professor was this total hard-ass who never gave A's. He always wore these tweed jackets with the elbow patches, even in the middle of summer. I don't know how he didn't sweat to death. But anyway, I'd be trying to memorize all these theories, and all I could hear was this crackly radio voice through the vent. I finally had to buy a white noise machine just to drown it out. It sounded like a waterfall, which was nice at first, but then it just made me have to use the bathroom all the time. But yeah, as far as hearing things that aren't actually there, like these voices at work... no, this is the first time. It's just happening now, with everything else.
Do you feel as guilty or critical of yourself in areas of your life outside of work, or is it mainly related to your job as a surveillance officer?

I mean, it's mostly work. Like I was telling you earlier, I just can't stop replaying every single missed camera angle or delayed call in my head. It just sits there like concrete proof that I'm completely careless, and... and dangerous, really. I still feel so strongly that I deserve to be punished if anything goes wrong on my watch. 

But outside of work... I don't know, I guess I don't do much outside of work right now to even mess up. I mostly just go home or go to the grocery store. I usually go to the one over on 4th Street because they have those new self-checkout lanes. I really hate waiting in line. Although, the last time I went, the scanner kept freezing when I tried to ring up my apples. I always buy Honeycrisp. They're so expensive now, though, like three or four dollars a pound, which is just ridiculous for fruit. 

My grandmother actually used to have an apple tree in her backyard when I was growing up. We'd pick them in the fall and she would make these huge, deep-dish pies completely from scratch. She had this special rolling pin made out of solid green marble. It was incredibly heavy, but she swore by it. She said the marble stayed cold and kept the butter from melting into the dough too fast. I actually inherited it when she passed away, but I don't bake at all. I just use it as a bookend on my living room shelf right now. I tried to make sugar cookies once for a charity bake sale back in high school, and I accidentally used salt instead of sugar. It was a total disaster, the principal actually spit it into a napkin. 

But yeah... I don't know. It's mostly just the surveillance job. That's where the guilt is the worst. I just feel like a hazard to everyone in the building.
Do you feel guilty or critical of yourself when you're not working, or is it mostly just related to things that happen on the job?

Well, like I was saying, it really is mostly work. I just... I can't stop replaying every missed camera angle or delayed call in my head. It just sits there like proof that I'm totally careless and dangerous, and part of me really believes I deserve to be punished if anything goes wrong on my watch. 

But when I'm not at work... I mean, I guess I just don't do much. I did go to the park the other day, just to sit on a bench. There was this lady feeding the ducks, which you're not really supposed to do, especially with bread. It's bad for their stomachs. I read this whole article about it in National Geographic once. My dad used to have a subscription, he kept stacks of those yellow magazines in the garage for years. He refused to throw them away because he said the photography was too good to put in the recycling bin. He actually wanted to be a photographer when he was younger, before he got drafted. He had this old Leica camera, the kind you had to manually wind. The leather strap was all worn out from him carrying it around everywhere. I think my sister has it now. She lives out in Seattle, works for some tech company. It rains so much out there, I don't know how she stands it. I need sunshine, even if I spend most of my time in a dark surveillance room. But yeah, the guilt... it's really just tied to the job and feeling like I'm putting everyone in danger.
Do you think the accusations made by the voices are based on actual mistakes you've made or are they exaggerating and being unfair?

I... I don't know if they're exaggerating, because that's exactly what scared me enough to finally come in here. It's when I'm in the surveillance room, and it's one of those quiet stretches. I'll hear these voices coming right through the monitor speakers. They say things like, "You missed it, Ruth," or "People are going to get hurt because of you." And the thing is, I check the channels, and every single one is completely muted. None of the other guards hear it. 

We actually got these new monitors last year. They're those curved screens, supposed to be better for your peripheral vision or something. The tech guys took a whole weekend to install them, and they left zip ties all over the floor. I almost tripped over one on a Monday morning. I had this thermos of coffee—it's one of those Yeti ones that keeps things hot for like twelve hours. My sister got it for me for my birthday. She got it engraved with my initials, which I thought was a little much, but it's a nice color, kind of a seafoam green. I used to love going to the beach when we were kids. We'd go to Cape May every summer and collect sea glass. My mom had this big glass jar in the kitchen window where she kept it all. It looked so pretty when the sun hit it in the late afternoon. 

But anyway, the voices... they just sound so clear coming through those speakers, even when everything is muted. It just makes me feel like I really am missing something terrible.
Do you think there's any possibility that the voices are wrong about you being careless and dangerous, or do you believe they are always telling the truth?

I mean... I don't think they're wrong. That's the awful part. I really don't think they're wrong at all. Like I said before, I just keep replaying every single missed camera angle, every delayed call... it just sits in my brain like absolute proof that I am completely careless. And dangerous. Part of me really believes I deserve to be punished if anything goes wrong on my watch, because it would be my fault. 

And fault is a funny thing, isn't it? Like with car accidents. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, he got into a fender bender last week right at the end of our street. The stop sign there is completely hidden by this massive oak tree. The city is supposed to trim it, but they never do. I called public works about it three times last spring. You get put on hold for forty-five minutes and then they just transfer you to a voicemail that's full. It's ridiculous. Mr. Henderson drives this pristine 1998 Buick LeSabre, too. He washes it every Sunday morning in his driveway, wearing these bright yellow rubber gloves. He used to be a plumber before he retired, so I guess he's used to wearing gloves. He actually helped me fix a leaky pipe under my kitchen sink a few years ago. It was just a worn-out washer, cost like fifty cents at the hardware store, but it saved me a huge plumbing bill. Plumbers charge so much just to walk through the door these days. 

But yeah, the voices... I just feel like they're telling the truth about me. I really do feel like I'm a danger to the people I'm supposed to be watching out for.
Do you think the voices are ever unfair or unrealistic in their criticism of you?

I don't think they're unfair, no. I mean... like I said, that's what scared me enough to finally come in here. It's when it's quiet in the surveillance room, and those voices come right through the monitor speakers. They tell me, "You missed it, Ruth," or "People are going to get hurt because of you." And it feels completely realistic because I *know* I could miss something. Even though I check the channels and they're all muted, and the other guards don't hear a thing... it just feels so real to me. 

The other guards, they usually just listen to podcasts anyway. My shift partner, Dave, he listens to these true crime ones for eight hours straight. I don't know how he does it. It would give me nightmares. I used to listen to the radio, back when they actually played music instead of just commercials and morning shows where people yell at each other. My mom had this old Zenith radio in the kitchen when I was growing up. It had this faux-wood paneling on the side that was peeling off at the corners. She'd listen to it while she made dinner. She made the best meatloaf. She put a little bit of brown sugar in the ketchup glaze on top, which sounds weird, but it was amazing. I tried to make it once, but I bought the wrong kind of ground beef—it was too lean, so it came out really dry. Ground beef has gotten so expensive lately anyway. Have you noticed that at the grocery store? I usually shop at the one on 4th Street, but they rearranged all the aisles last month and now I can't find the coffee filters. 

But no, I don't think the voices are being unfair. They're just saying what's true.
Do you think you would feel this guilty and critical of yourself if the voices weren't telling you these things?

I... I don't think so. Before this whole stretch of feeling so hopeless and guilty, right after they changed the surveillance lead at work... I had never heard accusations coming through the equipment like that. I never felt so absolutely certain that I was dangerous to everyone around me. It all just started together, the voices and these awful beliefs, they're all just part of this same terrible low period. 

The new lead, his name is Marcus. He came from a casino in Atlantic City, so he thinks he knows everything about everything. He wears these really strong colognes, the kind that linger in the elevator long after he's gotten off. It gives me a headache. I used to get migraines a lot in my twenties. I had to sit in a dark room with a cold washcloth over my eyes. My cat, Barnaby—he was an orange tabby, lived to be seventeen—he used to come sit on my chest and purr when I had a migraine. People say cats don't care about you, but they really do. They just show it differently than dogs. Dogs are so needy. My sister has a Golden Retriever that basically has to be touching you at all times or it starts whining. It sheds everywhere, too. You wear black pants to her house and you leave looking like you're growing fur. Lint rollers don't even make a dent in it. You have to use that packing tape trick, you know? Where you wrap it around your hand sticky-side out? 

But yeah, to answer your question, the voices and feeling like I'm this terrible danger... none of that happened before this whole awful slump started.
Do you feel guilty or critical of yourself in situations outside of your work as a surveillance officer?

I mean, it's mostly at work, but... it spills over, I guess. It's just this constant feeling I have now. Like I told you, I just keep replaying every single missed camera angle or delayed call in my head, over and over, like it's absolute proof that I am careless and dangerous. And part of me really believes I deserve to be punished if anything goes wrong on my watch. It's like this heavy weight I carry everywhere, not just in the surveillance room. 

It reminds me of when I used to carry my backpack in college. I went to the state university, and the campus was built on this massive hill. They called it "Cardiac Hill" because you'd be completely out of breath by the time you got to the science building at the top. I had this heavy canvas backpack, army green. I bought it at an army surplus store downtown. That store is closed now, they turned it into one of those artisanal donut shops where a single donut costs six dollars and has, like, bacon and maple syrup on it. I don't understand the appeal of bacon on a donut. Bacon should be crispy and served with eggs. My dad used to make eggs every Saturday morning. He had this special cast-iron skillet that he never washed with soap, just wiped it out with a paper towel. He said soap ruined the seasoning. Cast iron is so heavy, though. If you drop it, you could break a toe. I broke my pinky toe once by stubbing it on a coffee table, and there's really nothing they can do for a broken toe, they just tape it to the next toe. Buddy taping, they call it. 

But yeah, that feeling of being careless and dangerous... it's just always there, telling me I deserve to be punished.
Do you think anyone else would agree that you are as careless and dangerous as the voices say you are?

Would anyone else agree? I... I'm not really sure. Like I was just saying a minute ago, I'm the one who's constantly replaying every missed camera angle or delayed call in my head. To me, it's just undeniable proof that I'm careless and dangerous, and I really do believe I deserve to be punished if anything goes wrong on my watch. But if you asked Dave, my shift partner, he'd probably say I'm doing fine. 

Dave doesn't even look at the screens half the time, though. He's always staring at his phone. Everyone is glued to their phones these days. You go out to a restaurant and whole families are just sitting there staring at screens, not saying a single word to each other. It's kind of sad. I remember when phones were just attached to the kitchen wall with those long, coiled cords. We had this ugly mustard-yellow one when I was a kid, and the cord got so stretched out it would drag all over the linoleum floor. Linoleum is a nightmare to keep clean, by the way. If you use the wrong soap, it leaves this sticky film that traps all the dirt. I always just use white vinegar and warm water. Vinegar is basically a miracle cleaner. You can use it on windows, too, if you wipe it with crumpled-up newspaper so it doesn't streak. Though I guess nobody really gets the physical newspaper delivered anymore, do they? It's all on the internet now. My dad used to read the Sunday paper cover to cover... 

But... yeah, I don't know what other people would say about me at work. I just know what I see in myself, and I know I'm a danger.
Do you think the voices are the main reason you feel guilty and critical of yourself, or would you feel that way even if you didn't hear them?

I think... well, like I was telling you earlier, I just constantly keep replaying every missed camera angle or delayed call in my head. It's just undeniable proof to me that I am careless and dangerous. So even if the voices stopped right now, I'm pretty sure that part of me still truly believes I deserve to be punished if anything goes wrong on my watch. 

Punishment is... well, it just makes me think of this time I got a parking ticket downtown. The meter maid was practically hiding behind a mailbox just waiting for the time to expire. You know, mailboxes are really disappearing. The big blue ones on the street corners? You barely see them anymore. People just don't send letters. Everything is email or text message now. My aunt still sends physical birthday cards, though. She always puts a crisp five-dollar bill inside. I don't even know where she gets crisp bills, maybe she goes inside the actual bank and asks the teller specifically for new ones. Banks are always so freezing inside, the air conditioning is just blasting no matter what. You have to bring a sweater even in the middle of July. July gets so terribly humid here, it just completely ruins my hair... 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, I'd probably still feel like I deserve to be punished for being so careless, voices or no voices.
Do you think your belief that you deserve to be punished for your mistakes at work is an exaggerated or unrealistic one?

I don't think it's exaggerated. I mean, like I've said, I keep replaying every single missed camera angle or delayed call in my head, over and over. To me, it's just absolute proof that I am careless and dangerous. And part of me really believes I deserve to be punished if anything goes wrong on my watch. It's a huge responsibility, watching those monitors. 

Monitors have gotten so flat now. I remember when TVs and computer screens were these huge, heavy boxes that took up the whole desk. We had this old desktop computer in the nineties, it took like ten minutes just to connect to the internet with that awful screeching dial-up sound. And you couldn't use the phone at the same time. If someone picked up the receiver in the kitchen, it would completely knock you offline. My sister used to do that to me on purpose when I was trying to chat with my friends on AOL. She was always so annoying, she used to steal my clothes without asking and stretch out the collars. I had this one favorite sweater, it was a really soft angora wool, light pink. You have to hand wash angora or it completely ruins the texture. Hand washing is such a chore, though. I have this special basin I use just for delicates, I bought it at a yard sale years ago. Yard sales are great, but you have to get up at the crack of dawn to find anything good. The early bird gets the worm, my grandmother always used to say. She loved birds. She had this bird feeder outside her kitchen window and would sit there for hours just watching the cardinals and the blue jays... 

But, um, no, I don't think it's unrealistic at all. I really am dangerous, and I deserve whatever punishment comes to me.

He was this little terrier mix, scruffy, always full of energy. His name was Buster. Anyway, I left the front door cracked open while I was grabbing the mail, and he just bolted. I spent three hours running around the neighborhood crying, shaking a bag of treats. We finally found him at the park two blocks over, chasing ducks into the pond. He was completely soaked and smelled terrible, like algae and mud. My roommate was so mad at me, she wouldn't speak to me for a week. She ended up moving out at the end of the semester. She transferred to a school out of state, actually. Somewhere in Colorado, I think. She always wanted to learn how to snowboard. But yeah, when I hear those voices at work, it's that same feeling. I remember when phones were just attached to the kitchen wall with those long, coiled cords. We had this ugly mustard-yellow one when I was a kid, and the cord got so stretched out it would drag all over the linoleum floor. Linoleum is a nightmare to keep clean, by the way. If you use the wrong soap, it leaves this sticky film that traps all the dirt. I always just use white vinegar and warm water. Vinegar is basically a miracle cleaner. You can use it on windows, too, if you wipe it with crumpled-up newspaper so it doesn't streak. Though I guess nobody really gets the physical newspaper delivered anymore, do they? It's all on the internet now. My dad used to read the Sunday paper cover to cover... 

But... yeah, I don't know what other people would say about me at work. I just know what I see in myself, and I know I'm a danger.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's guilt and self-criticism are delusional
doctor.question: Do you think the voices are the main reason you feel guilty and critical of yourself, or would you feel that way even if you didn't hear them?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep replaying every missed camera angle or delayed call like proof that I am careless and dangerous, and part of me believes I deserve to be punished if anything goes wrong on my watch.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the patient's feelings of guilt are independent of the hallucinations, which is an assessment of the nature and validity of the worthlessness/guilt symptom.

patient.answer:
I think... well, like I was telling you earlier, I just constantly keep replaying every missed camera angle or delayed call in my head. It's just undeniable proof to me that I am careless and dangerous. So even if the voices stopped right now, I'm pretty sure that part of me still truly believes I deserve to be punished if anything goes wrong on my watch. 

Punishment is... well, it just makes me think of this time I got a parking ticket downtown. The meter maid was practically hiding behind a mailbox just waiting for the time to expire. You know, mailboxes are really disappearing. The big blue ones on the street corners? You barely see them anymore. People just don't send letters. Everything is email or text message now. My aunt still sends physical birthday cards, though. She always puts a crisp five-dollar bill inside. I don't even know where she gets crisp bills, maybe she goes inside the actual bank and asks the teller specifically for new ones. Banks are always so freezing inside, the air conditioning is just blasting no matter what. You have to bring a sweater even in the middle of July. July gets so terribly humid here, it just completely ruins my hair... 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, I'd probably still feel like I deserve to be punished for being so careless, voices or no voices.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's guilt and self-criticism are delusional
doctor.question: Do you think your belief that you deserve to be punished for your mistakes at work is an exaggerated or unrealistic one?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep replaying every missed camera angle or delayed call like proof that I am careless and dangerous, and part of me believes I deserve to be punished if anything goes wrong on my watch.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether my belief that I deserve to be punished for mistakes is exaggerated or unrealistic, which directly probes the delusional or excessive nature of my guilt.

patient.answer:
I don't think it's exaggerated. I mean, like I've said, I keep replaying every single missed camera angle or delayed call in my head, over and over. To me, it's just absolute proof that I am careless and dangerous. And part of me really believes I deserve to be punished if anything goes wrong on my watch. It's a huge responsibility, watching those monitors. 

Monitors have gotten so flat now. I remember when TVs and computer screens were these huge, heavy boxes that took up the whole desk. We had this old desktop computer in the nineties, it took like ten minutes just to connect to the internet with that awful screeching dial-up sound. And you couldn't use the phone at the same time. If someone picked up the receiver in the kitchen, it would completely knock you offline. My sister used to do that to me on purpose when I was trying to chat with my friends on AOL. She was always so annoying, she used to steal my clothes without asking and stretch out the collars. I had this one favorite sweater, it was a really soft angora wool, light pink. You have to hand wash angora or it completely ruins the texture. Hand washing is such a chore, though. I have this special basin I use just for delicates, I bought it at a yard sale years ago. Yard sales are great, but you have to get up at the crack of dawn to find anything good. The early bird gets the worm, my grandmother always used to say. She loved birds. She had this bird feeder outside her kitchen window and would sit there for hours just watching the cardinals and the blue jays... 

But, um, no, I don't think it's unrealistic at all. I really am dangerous, and I deserve whatever punishment comes to me.
